title: Knight moves and board display
instructions:
Implement a rectangular chess-knight move helper and a plain-text board printer.

## Files
- `knight_board.py`

- `parse_square(square: str, width: int, height: int) -> tuple[int, int]` converts
  notation to zero-based `(x, y)` coordinates. Notation must be one lowercase
  ASCII letter followed by a positive ASCII decimal rank without leading zeros
  (`a1`, `h8`, `z99`). The square must be within the supplied dimensions; otherwise
  raise `ValueError`. Assume valid dimensions for this helper and string squares.
- `format_square(x: int, y: int) -> str` performs the inverse. Assume valid
  zero-based coordinates with `0 <= x < 26` and `0 <= y < 99`.
- `KnightBoard(width: int = 8, height: int = 8)` accepts exact integers (bool is
  invalid), with width 1–26 and height 1–99. Wrong types raise `TypeError`; integer
  values outside these bounds raise `ValueError`.
- `moves(start: str, blocked=()) -> list[str]`: all legal destinations exactly
  `(1, 2)` or `(2, 1)` away, with either sign on each offset. Keep only squares
  inside the board and not blocked. Return notation sorted by increasing rank,
  then increasing file (coordinate order, not lexicographic order of strings).
- `render(start: str, blocked=()) -> str`: print ranks from height down to 1 and
  files left to right. Cells are `K` for start, `#` for blocked, `*` for an
  unblocked legal destination, and `.` otherwise, in that priority. Join cells
  with one space and rows with `\n`, with no final newline or labels.

Both methods validate start and every blocked square with `parse_square`, raising
`ValueError` for invalid notation/out-of-board squares. `blocked` is any iterable
of square strings, possibly a generator or containing duplicates. It may contain
start: the knight is still allowed to move and its displayed cell remains `K`.
Blocked squares affect destinations only; knights jump over other pieces.
